case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
case.limits: It drew one of the most cited dissents in intellectual property, warning that overprotecting identity taxes the public domain, and later courts have policed its edges. It is powerful in advertising contexts and contested everywhere else.
case.holding: A robot dressed and posed to evoke Vanna White in an advertisement could violate her right of publicity, because the right protects identity however it is evoked, not just name, likeness or voice.
case.case_name: White v. Samsung Electronics America, Inc.
case.why_ai_cites_it: The case that stretched publicity rights to cover evocation by machine. Plaintiffs cite it for the claim that an AI rendering need not copy a face or voice to appropriate a person, resembling them in the ways that identify them is enough, which is the outer theory in digital-replica and deepfake suits.

reading.body:
The most consequential thing *White v. Samsung* established for AI is that appropriation does not require copying: evoking a person's identity, by any means, can be enough to trigger a right of publicity claim.

The Ninth Circuit held in 1992 that a robot styled to suggest Vanna White, without using her name, image, or voice, could still violate her rights because the right of publicity protects identity however it is evoked. That logic maps directly onto AI-generated content. A synthesized rendering that resembles someone in the ways that identify them, without lifting a face or cloning a voice, falls within the theory the case opened. Plaintiffs in digital-replica and deepfake suits cite it for exactly that outer reach.

The case carries its own caveat. It drew one of the most cited dissents in intellectual property law, on the ground that overprotecting identity burdens the public domain, and later courts have confined it. Its force is clearest in advertising contexts, the setting where it arose, and more contested when plaintiffs try to extend it elsewhere. The data does not say which AI disputes have succeeded on this theory, only that plaintiffs reach for it. What the case does and does not authorize in practice remains a live question that subsequent decisions, not this one, will have to answer.
